---
title: "Rules, state, and undo: the bracelet"
---

A friendship bracelet is a row of beads, and a row of beads is a list. What
makes it interesting is that not every list is a legal bracelet: a letter cube,
then a spacer bead, then a letter cube, and so on. This chapter has no new
keyword in it. It is about where a rule like that lives, and about the design
decision that turns undo into two lines.

## Two ways to keep a list {#sec-bracelet-experiment}

Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/`. Replace the body of
`index.html` with this, keeping the `<script>` line at the end:

```html
<h1>Word list</h1>

<input id="wordInput" type="text">
<button type="button" id="addButton">Add</button>
<button type="button" id="undoButton">Undo</button>

<ul id="list"></ul>
```

Now put this into `src/index.ts`:

```ts
const list = document.querySelector<HTMLUListElement>('#list');
const wordInput = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#wordInput');
const addButton = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('#addButton');
const undoButton = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('#undoButton');
if (!list || !wordInput || !addButton || !undoButton) {
  throw new Error('An element is missing from index.html');
}

addButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  const item = document.createElement('li');
  item.textContent = wordInput.value;
  list.append(item);
  wordInput.value = '';
});

undoButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  const last = list.lastElementChild;
  if (last) {
    last.remove();
  }
});
```

Run `npm start`, type three words, add each one, and press Undo twice. It
works. `lastElementChild` hands you the last element inside `#list`, or `null`
when the list is empty, and `remove()` takes it out of the tree.

Now find where this app keeps the words. There is no array and no variable
holding them: they live in the page, in the `<li>` elements, and the only way
to find out what the user built is to read the page back.

## The same list from an array {#sec-bracelet-array}

Keep `index.html` and the lookups at the top, and replace the two listeners
with this:

```ts
const words: string[] = [];

const render = () => {
  list.replaceChildren();
  for (const word of words) {
    const item = document.createElement('li');
    item.textContent = word;
    list.append(item);
  }
};

addButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  words.push(wordInput.value);
  wordInput.value = '';
  render();
});

undoButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  words.pop();
  render();
});
```

The page behaves exactly as before. What changed is where the words live: in
`words`, an array your program owns. `render()` throws every `<li>` away with
`replaceChildren()` and builds the list again from the array, the way the
bubble chart in the SVG part redrew itself after every new bubble.

Neither listener touches an `<li>` any more. Both of them change `words` and
then ask `render()` to draw the whole list again.

## Adding a rule {#sec-bracelet-rule}

Give the word list a rule: the same word twice in a row is not allowed.

The version that edits the page directly has to ask the page what it shows:

```ts
const last = list.lastElementChild;
if (last && last.textContent === wordInput.value) {
  return;
}
```

That works, and look at what it costs. The rule is about words, but the code is
about elements: a `string | null` your own program put there earlier, plus a
separate case for the empty list. Every further rule means another walk through
the DOM.

The version that keeps a `words` array reads like the rule itself:

```ts
if (wordInput.value === words[words.length - 1]) {
  return;
}
```

The array is the truth, and the page is only a picture of it.

## Model first {#sec-bracelet-model}

The `words` array of the word list is a **model**: the data your app is really
about, plus the rules that say which states are allowed. In this part of the
book a model is a class, or a small set of classes; the bracelet editor's model
is a `Bracelet` class that holds the items. Three habits go with it, and every
app in this chapter and the next follows them.

**The model owns the state and the rules.** Nothing outside the model may push
into its array. A method such as `addLetter` is the only door, and that door
checks.

**The whole picture is drawn from the model after every change.** One `render`
method empties the container and builds it again. It never patches, so the
page can never drift away from the data.

**A move the model refuses is an exception.** `addLetter` throws a `RuleError`
of your own, exactly as the calculator's logic did in the chapter on
exceptions, and the code that wired up the button catches it and puts
`error.message` on the page. The model never decides where a message goes.

Not every complaint is a refusal, though. Putting a green bead next to a row of
red ones is allowed, it just deserves a comment. That is a return value, not a
`throw`: `addSpacer` puts the bead on the string and hands back a warning text,
or `undefined` when it has nothing to say. Throw when the operation did not
happen. Return a value when it did.

Undo falls out of this for free. Take the last item off the array, render
again. The model needs no memory of what the user did, because the array is
the memory.

::: {.callout-note}
## One compromise, on purpose

The `Bracelet` class still knows one DOM element: the container it draws into.
A model that knows nothing about the page is easier to test, and the part on
testing splits this class in two for exactly that reason. For now, keeping the
drawing inside the model keeps the wiring short.
:::

## The bracelet on paper {#sec-bracelet-design}

Four classes carry the whole editor, and the diagram is worth drawing before
any of them is typed.

![The bracelet on one page: `Bracelet` holds many `BraceletItem`, `LetterCube`
and `SpacerBead` are the two kinds of item, and both adding methods throw a
`RuleError`, an error class of your own that extends
`Error`.](bracelet-classes.svg){width=660}

Read the middle box first. `BraceletItem` is abstract and promises one thing:
every item can build the element that shows it. `Bracelet` holds
`BraceletItem[]`, so it never mentions `LetterCube` or `SpacerBead` when it
renders. It loops over the array and calls `render()` on whatever is in there,
which is polymorphism doing real work. The two `render` methods in the picture
do different jobs: an item builds one element and hands it back, and the
bracelet's private one empties the container and collects them all.

The rule itself needs one question answered: which kind of item is the last one
on the string? An empty bracelet expects a letter cube. After a letter cube a
spacer bead is due, and after a spacer bead a letter cube. That is the entire
pattern, and it depends only on the last item.

::: {.research title="Reading the end of an array, and a button with no text"}
Your undo removes the last item, your rule asks what the last item is, your
letter buttons come from one string, and your color buttons carry no text at
all. MDN has all four answers.

1. `for (const letter of 'ABC')` walks over a string. What is `letter` in each
   round, and what does the loop do when the string is empty?
2. `pop()` takes the last element out of an array. What does it give back, and
   what happens when you call it on an array that is already empty?
3. `at(-1)` reads the last element of an array. What do you get from `at(-1)`
   when the array is empty, and what does `array[-1]` give you instead?
4. Your color buttons have a background color and nothing inside them, so
   somebody using a screen reader hears nothing useful. What does an
   `aria-label` attribute change for them, and why does a sighted visitor never
   see it?

For the exam, remember what `pop()` does to an empty array. Your undo button
calls it whether the bracelet holds anything or not.
:::

## Exercise: the friendship bracelet editor {#sec-bracelet-exercise}

Letter cubes and spacer beads on a string, with the alternating rule, a warning
about mixed colors, and a "Remove last" button.

{{< exercise bracelet >}}

1. Create a new app from our template inside `homework/`, in a folder called
   `bracelet`. Read the `index.html` you copied in: a `#preview` box with an
   empty `<div id="bracelet">` inside it, a `<p id="message">` for errors and
   warnings, two empty containers `#letterGrid` and `#colorRow` that your code
   fills with buttons, and `#undoButton`.

2. Create `src/bracelet-item.ts` with the promise every item makes:

   ```ts
   export abstract class BraceletItem {
     abstract render(): HTMLElement;
   }
   ```

3. Create `src/letter-cube.ts`. `LetterCube` extends `BraceletItem`, takes the
   letter in its constructor, and keeps it in a private field. Its `render()`
   creates a `<div>`, adds the class `cube` to it, puts the letter in as
   `textContent`, and returns it. The stylesheet already knows `.cube`.

4. Create `src/spacer-bead.ts`. `SpacerBead` works the same way with a color
   instead of a letter: class `bead`, and the color goes into
   `bead.style.backgroundColor`. Declare the field as `readonly color: string`,
   without `private`. The `Bracelet` class needs to read it in step 6, and
   `readonly` still stops anybody from changing it.

5. Create `src/rule-error.ts` with an error class of your own:

   ```ts
   export class RuleError extends Error {
     constructor(message: string) {
       super(message);
       this.name = 'RuleError';
     }
   }
   ```

6. Create `src/bracelet.ts`. The `Bracelet` class holds three private fields: a
   `BraceletItem[]` that starts empty, the container element, and a boolean
   that remembers whether the color warning has already been shown. Its
   constructor takes the container element and renders once. Then these
   methods:

   * `addLetter(letter: string): void` throws
     `new RuleError('You need to add a spacer bead next!')` when a spacer bead
     is due. Otherwise it pushes a new `LetterCube` and renders.
   * `addSpacer(color: string): string | undefined` throws
     `new RuleError('You need to add a letter cube next!')` when a letter cube
     is due. Otherwise it pushes a new `SpacerBead` and renders. When the
     bracelet already carries a spacer bead in a different color and the
     warning has not been shown yet, it remembers that it has now been shown
     and returns `'You are mixing spacer colors!'`. In every other case it
     returns `undefined`.
   * `removeLast(): void` pops the array and renders.
   * A private method that answers whether a letter cube is due. Read the last
     item and decide: nothing there means a letter cube, a `SpacerBead` means a
     letter cube, anything else means a spacer bead.
   * A private method that answers whether the bracelet already carries a
     spacer bead in some other color. Loop over the items and test each one
     with `item instanceof SpacerBead`. Asking what kind of thing you have is
     fine here, because the answer is a fact about the bracelet, not a choice
     between two behaviors.
   * A private `render()` that calls `replaceChildren()` on the container and
     appends `item.render()` for every item.

   `BraceletItem` appears only after a colon in this file, so its import is
   `import type { BraceletItem } from './bracelet-item';`.

7. Replace everything in `src/index.ts`. It imports the stylesheet, `Bracelet`,
   and `RuleError`, and it holds no class of its own. Start with the two lists:

   ```ts
   const LETTERS = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ♥★';
   const SPACER_COLORS = [
     { name: 'rose', value: '#f4a0a0' },
     { name: 'sand', value: '#f4d4a0' },
     { name: 'mint', value: '#a0d4a0' },
     { name: 'blue', value: '#a0a0f4' },
     { name: 'lilac', value: '#d4a0f4' },
     { name: 'pink', value: '#f4a0d4' },
     { name: 'aqua', value: '#a0f4f4' },
     { name: 'lime', value: '#d4f4a0' },
     { name: 'peach', value: '#f4c8a0' },
   ];
   ```

8. Look up `#bracelet`, `#message`, `#letterGrid`, `#colorRow`, and
   `#undoButton` with one null check that throws, then create the bracelet with
   `new Bracelet(braceletBox)` and write a small `showMessage(text: string)`
   helper that sets the paragraph's `textContent`.

9. Build the letter grid: one `<button>` per letter, with `type` set to
   `'button'`, the letter as its text, and a click listener. Build the color
   row: one `<button>` per entry of `SPACER_COLORS`, with its `value` as the
   background color and an `aria-label` that names the color, so the button
   says something without carrying text.

10. Wire the clicks. A letter click calls `bracelet.addLetter(letter)` inside a
    `try` and clears the message afterwards. Its `catch` shows `error.message`
    when the error `instanceof RuleError`, and re-throws anything else, because
    an error you did not plan for must not disappear. A color click does the
    same around `bracelet.addSpacer(color)` and shows the returned warning when
    it is not `undefined`. The undo button calls `bracelet.removeLast()` and
    clears the message.

11. Run `npm start` and try all of it. Expected results: a letter cube appears
    on the string; a second letter right after it leaves the bracelet
    untouched and shows "You need to add a spacer bead next!"; a spacer bead on
    the empty bracelet shows "You need to add a letter cube next!"; a bead in a
    second color is added and shows "You are mixing spacer colors!" once and
    never again; "Remove last" takes items off one at a time and does nothing
    on an empty bracelet.

12. Run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

## The same skeleton, other names {#sec-bracelet-skeleton}

A sandwich stacker asks for an ingredient layer, then a sauce stripe, then an
ingredient layer. Other words, same four classes: an abstract layer with
`render()`, two subclasses that know how to draw themselves, a `Sandwich` that
holds the array and refuses the wrong move, and an `index.ts` that catches the
refusal and shows it. Build the bracelet from an empty folder once and you can
build that one too, which is worth practicing before a lesson where the
internet and the agent are switched off.
